passed.title: Datetime time unit is inferred from the format string
passed.trap: When you give a format, `Expr.str.to_datetime` and `Expr.str.strptime` infer the time unit from it. `%.3f` yields `Datetime("ms")`; with no fractional seconds the default is `"us"`. Columns parsed with different formats can therefore end up with different `Datetime` dtypes. Pass `time_unit=` to `Expr.str.to_datetime` to pin the unit, for example `time_unit="ns"`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["2024-01-01 00:00:00.123"]})
fmt = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%.3f"
inferred = df.select(pl.col("s").str.to_datetime(fmt))
pinned = df.select(pl.col("s").str.to_datetime(fmt, time_unit="ns"))
print(inferred.schema)
print(pinned.schema)
passed.output:
Schema({'s': Datetime(time_unit='ms', time_zone=None)})
Schema({'s': Datetime(time_unit='ns', time_zone=None)})

passed.title: strip_chars_start strips a character set, not a prefix
passed.trap: `Expr.str.strip_chars_start` treats its argument as a **set** of characters and strips any leading combination of them. So `"fo"` turns `"foofoobar"` into `"bar"` and `"ooze"` into `"ze"`. Once you pass `characters`, leading whitespace is no longer stripped. To remove an exact prefix once, use `Expr.str.strip_prefix`, or `Expr.str.strip_suffix` for the end. If the whole string equals the prefix or suffix, the result is an empty string, not null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": ["foofoobar", "ooze", " foo", "foo", "bar"]})
out = df.with_columns(
    chars=pl.col("a").str.strip_chars_start("fo"),
    prefix=pl.col("a").str.strip_prefix("foo"),
    suffix=pl.col("a").str.strip_suffix("bar"),
)
print(out["a"].to_list())
print(out["chars"].to_list())
print(out["prefix"].to_list())
print(out["suffix"].to_list())

passed.title: to_integer raises on bad input unless strict=False
passed.trap: `Expr.str.to_integer` defaults to `strict=True`, so one unparsable string makes the whole query raise. Pass `strict=False` to turn failures into null instead. Use `base=` for binary or hex input. Use `dtype=` to choose the integer type; the default is `Int64`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["12", "abc", None]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("s").str.to_integer())
except Exception as e:
    print("raised:", type(e))
out = df.select(pl.col("s").str.to_integer(strict=False))
print(out["s"].to_list())
hexdf = pl.DataFrame({"h": ["ff", "10"]})
hx = hexdf.select(pl.col("h").str.to_integer(base=16, dtype=pl.Int32))
print(hx["h"].to_list())
print(hx.schema)

passed.title: Date parsing is strict and exact by default
passed.trap: `Expr.str.to_date`, `Expr.str.to_datetime` and `Expr.str.strptime` default to `strict=True`. One invalid value, such as `2024-02-30`, raises instead of becoming null. They also default to `exact=True`, so any text around the date makes parsing fail. Use `strict=False` to get nulls for bad rows. Use `exact=False` to match the format anywhere in the string, at a performance cost.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["2024-01-05", "2024-02-30", "due 2024-03-01"]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("s").str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d"))
except Exception as e:
    print("raised:", type(e))
out = df.select(
    lenient=pl.col("s").str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d", strict=False),
    anywhere=pl.col("s").str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d", strict=False, exact=False),
)
print(out["lenient"].to_list())
print(out["anywhere"].to_list())

passed.title: time_zone replaces naive times but converts offset-aware ones
passed.trap: In `Expr.str.to_datetime`, the `time_zone` argument behaves differently depending on the input. For tz-naive strings it **replaces** the zone, so 12:00 stays 12:00 local time. For strings with an offset it **converts**, so 12:00+0000 becomes 17:30 in Asia/Kolkata. Offset-aware input without `time_zone` comes back in UTC. Check whether your strings carry an offset before assuming which behaviour you get.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

naive = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["2024-01-01 12:00"]})
aware = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["2024-01-01 12:00+0000"]})
replaced = naive.select(
    pl.col("s").str.to_datetime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", time_zone="Asia/Kolkata")
).item()
converted = aware.select(
    pl.col("s").str.to_datetime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M%z", time_zone="Asia/Kolkata")
).item()
print(replaced)
print(converted)
print(aware.select(pl.col("s").str.to_datetime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M%z")).schema)

passed.title: to_decimal is unstable and requires scale
passed.trap: `Expr.str.to_decimal` is marked unstable and may change without notice. Since 1.33.0, `inference_length` has been removed and the keyword-only `scale` is mandatory. Older code that calls it with no arguments now fails with a `TypeError`. Always pass `scale=`. Values with fewer decimals are padded, so `143.9` becomes `143.90` at scale 2.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": ["40.12", "143.9"]})
try:
    df.select(pl.col("x").str.to_decimal())
except Exception as e:
    print("raised:", type(e))
out = df.select(pl.col("x").str.to_decimal(scale=2))
print(out["x"].to_list())
print(out.schema)

passed.title: Use zfill, not pad_start, for signed numbers
passed.trap: `Expr.str.zfill` inserts zeros **after** a leading `-`, giving `-001`. `Expr.str.pad_start` with `"0"` puts the zeros before the sign, giving the wrong `00-1`. Both are string methods, so cast numeric columns to `pl.String` first. `Expr.str.zfill` is intended for numeric strings; for non-ASCII text the docs recommend `Expr.str.pad_start`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [-1, 123, None]})
s = pl.col("a").cast(pl.String)
out = df.with_columns(zfill=s.str.zfill(4), pad=s.str.pad_start(4, "0"))
print(out["zfill"].to_list())
print(out["pad"].to_list())

passed.title: Negative n in str.tail drops leading characters
passed.trap: `Expr.str.tail(-3)` does not mean the same as Python's `s[-3:]`. It returns everything **except the first 3** characters, like `s[3:]`. Use a positive `n` to get the last n characters. `n` counts characters, not bytes. Strings shorter than `n` come back whole, and nulls stay null.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"s": ["dragonfruit", "kiwi", "h\u00e9llo", None]})
out = df.with_columns(
    last3=pl.col("s").str.tail(3),
    neg3=pl.col("s").str.tail(-3),
    last4=pl.col("s").str.tail(4),
)
print(ascii(out["last3"].to_list()))
print(ascii(out["neg3"].to_list()))
print(ascii(out["last4"].to_list()))
